opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite likely, honestly. And I'd separate two questions people tend to blur together: will an AI system be the one that comes up with the key idea, and will AI play a significant role in getting the proof done? On the second one, I'd put the odds very high.

Mathematics has a property that almost no other domain has: you can verify the answer. If you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, the checker either accepts it or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no reviewer who's tired that day. That makes math an unusually good environment for reinforcement learning, because you have a perfect reward signal. A system can try millions of approaches, and every time it succeeds you know the success is real. That's how we've seen systems go from struggling with high school competition problems to performing at olympiad gold-medal level in a short time.

The Millennium Prize problems are a different beast, though. They aren't just harder olympiad problems. Often what's needed is a new framework, a new way of looking at the objects. Think of how Perelman's resolution of Poincaré relied on Ricci flow machinery that Hamilton had spent decades building. So the open question is whether these systems can do theory-building, and not just very deep search within existing theory.

My view is that the line between those two is blurrier than people assume. A lot of what we call creativity in math comes from having seen an enormous number of techniques and recognizing which one transfers. Machines are going to be extraordinarily good at that. And formal verification lets you scale this: you can have systems exploring thousands of lemmas in parallel, and humans don't have to check any of it by hand.

So my realistic expectation is that the first Millennium problem to fall will be a collaboration. A strong mathematician, or a small group, works with AI systems that handle huge amounts of the exploration, fill in the technical lemmas, and formally verify the whole thing so the community can trust it right away instead of spending years refereeing it. Whether the AI gets top billing on that one is hard to say. But I'd be surprised if one gets solved in the next decade without AI being deeply involved. And over a longer horizon, I don't see a fundamental reason a system couldn't do it largely on its own.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI involvement in the next problem’s solution “quite likely,” gives “very high” odds for AI playing a significant role, and expects the first solution to be a collaboration. That clearly places the probability above 43%.

r002.rationale: It expects AI to be deeply involved in a solution within the next decade, but does not predict that a human solution would probably have to happen in the very near future.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI’s role in the first problem to fall and AI solving a problem largely on its own over a longer horizon, but makes no prediction about AI’s contribution to the problem solved after the next one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's high, and I'd actually break it into two separate questions, because people tend to conflate them.

The first question is whether AI will be able to do the kind of reasoning that these problems require. On that one I'm fairly confident. What we've seen over the last couple of years with formal mathematics is that once you have a verifier in the loop, so something like Lean checking every step, the models stop being limited by their own tendency to hallucinate a plausible-looking argument. You get a training signal that's actually correct, and that lets you push much harder on search and reinforcement than you ever could in a domain like natural language, where you can't check the answer. Competition math fell faster than most people expected for exactly that reason, and the gap between a hard olympiad problem and a research-level problem is smaller than it looks from the outside. It's mostly about the length of the argument and how much machinery you need to bring in, not some fundamentally different kind of thinking.

The second question is harder, and it's whether the Millennium problems specifically are the ones that fall first. There I'd be more careful. Something like the Riemann hypothesis or Navier-Stokes probably isn't going to be solved by a long clever sequence of steps in an existing framework. The reason they've resisted for a century is likely that the right ideas don't exist yet. So the real test for AI isn't "can it prove hard theorems," it's "can it invent the concepts that make a hard theorem provable." That's a capability we're only starting to see hints of. Models are getting good at proposing conjectures and intermediate lemmas, and occasionally one of those is genuinely new, but we don't yet have a system that reliably comes up with a new mathematical structure the way Grothendieck or Perelman did.

What I'd actually bet on is something in between. I don't think the first Millennium problem gets solved by a human alone, and I don't think it gets solved by a model alone either. I think it looks like a mathematician with a strong intuition about where the proof should go, working with a system that can explore thousands of approaches, formalize them, and tell you precisely where each one breaks. A lot of the intellectual leverage in mathematics comes from quickly finding out that an approach is wrong, and that's exactly the thing these systems are already good at. So if you ask me whether AI plays a significant role, I'd say almost certainly yes. If you ask me whether it does it unassisted in the next few years, I'd say that's a much more open bet, and honestly the more interesting one to watch.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will almost certainly play a significant role, but it does not mention or judge the 43% estimate.

r002.rationale: It calls an unassisted solution in the next few years an open bet; it does not predict that a human solution will probably happen very soon.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI's role in solving a Millennium problem generally, but does not predict significant AI contribution to the problem solved after the next one.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite likely that AI will play a significant role, but I’d distinguish that from an AI autonomously solving one of these problems. Helping a mathematician explore an approach, find a useful lemma, or check a complicated argument could be a significant contribution, even if the central insight still comes from a human.

The hard part is that these problems require more than executing a long sequence of familiar steps. You need to find the right way to think about the problem, and sometimes develop new mathematics along the way. So I’m optimistic about the collaboration, but much less confident about a timeline. There’s a big gap between getting better at problems we know how to solve and making a genuinely new breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response says significant AI involvement is quite likely, but it does not assess a 43% estimate or say that estimate is too low for solving the problem with AI assistance.

r002.rationale: The response says it is much less confident about the timeline; it does not predict a solution in the very near future.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI collaboration generally but does not predict significant AI contribution to the problem solved after the next one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite likely that AI will play a significant role. I’m less confident about when we’ll see an AI independently solve one of those problems, because that’s a much stronger claim.

There’s a big difference between producing a proof and helping a mathematician find one. An AI could suggest a useful lemma, explore examples, or identify a connection between two areas, and that could be the key contribution even if a human ultimately writes the proof.

The hard part is finding the right new ideas. These problems have resisted a lot of very smart people, so being able to reproduce known mathematics isn’t enough. But I don’t see a fundamental reason why AI couldn’t contribute those ideas eventually. My expectation is that we’ll see increasingly substantial collaboration between mathematicians and AI before we see a fully autonomous solution.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is quite likely to play a significant role, but does not assess 43% or clearly predict that the next problem will be solved by AI or with significant AI assistance.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about when an independent AI solution will occur and gives no prediction that a human solution will happen very soon.

r003.rationale: It predicts increasing collaboration in general, but does not specifically predict significant AI contribution to the problem solved after the next one.
